noticeAndWonder.context: Quick review from Lesson 7.7: Detective Chen is comparing two case notes. Note A says: 'The evidence locker holds exactly 54 files, split equally among 6 shelves.' Note B says: 'The surveillance van must stay parked for no more than 45 minutes.' Look closely at the phrases 'split equally... exactly' in Note A versus 'no more than' in Note B. What do you notice about how the wording is different, and what do you wonder about which situations need an equation with an equal sign versus an inequality?
wonderStarters: I wonder what would happen if…

revealWordProblem.title: (Review from 7.7) Apply: Overtime Hours Limit
revealWordProblem.text: Detective Chen's team can use at most 40 hours of overtime this week to close the case. So far the team has logged 26 hours. Write an inequality for the additional overtime hours t the team can still use, solve it, and graph the solution set on a number line.
revealWordProblem.sampleAnswer: The inequality is 26 + t ≤ 40. Subtracting 26 from both sides: t ≤ 40 − 26 = 14. Since ≤ includes the boundary, graph a closed circle at 14 and shade left (toward smaller values), meaning the team can use 14 or fewer additional overtime hours this week.

conceptIntro.heading: The Big Ideas — Lessons 7.4–7.7
conceptIntro.intro: Here is the one thing to remember from each lesson, plus a quick guided example. If one of these feels shaky, that lesson is right above this one in the menu — you can open it any time.
conceptIntro.keyIdea: 7.4: 'At least' means ≥ and 'at most' means ≤; 'more than' means > and 'fewer/less than' means <. • 7.5: Closed circle for ≤ or ≥ (included), open circle for < or > (not included); shade right for greater, left for less. • 7.6: Solve with inverse operations, then graph the solution set: open circle for < or >, closed for ≤ or ≥. • 7.7: 'Equals' or 'exactly' points to an equation (=); 'at least, at most, more than, fewer than' points to an inequality.

explore.instructions: Review from Lesson 7.7: Read each word problem. Decide if it needs an equation or an inequality. Write the mathematical model, solve it, and check your answer for reasonableness.

rows.wordProblem: A detective splits 42 clues equally among 6 case boards. How many clues per board?
rows.reasonable: Yes — 7 clues per board makes sense.

rows.wordProblem: A witness says the suspect carried fewer than 10 items. If the suspect already had 3, how many more could they carry?
rows.reasonable: Yes — up to 6 more items is reasonable.

rows.wordProblem: The evidence room needs at least 50 storage bins. They already have 28. How many more do they need?
rows.reasonable: Yes — at least 22 more bins makes sense.

hints: If the problem uses 'is,' 'equals,' or 'gives exactly,' use an equation (=). If it uses 'at least,' 'at most,' 'more than,' or 'fewer than,' use an inequality.
After solving, ask: Does my answer make sense in the real-world context? Could the number be negative? A fraction of a person?
explore.label: For each word problem, write the model, solve, and check for reasonableness.

discourse.prompt: How do you decide whether a word problem needs an equation or an inequality?
discourse.sentenceFrame: I use an equation when the problem says ___, but I use an inequality when the problem says ___ because ___.

optional.instructions: (Lesson 7.4) Each case clue describes a boundary. Drag every scenario into the inequality symbol it matches.

items.text: The getaway driver was going more than 70 mph
More than 6 fingerprints were on the safe
The ransom note was written under 3 minutes ago
Fewer than 9 cars left the parking lot
At least 30 dollars in coins was stolen
No fewer than 4 witnesses saw the suspect
At most 14 footprints were found in the mud
No more than 7 keys can open the vault

optional.hint: Sort by the key operation or concept each item shows.

optional.stem: (Lesson 7.5) Clue: the witness ran more than 15 feet, so d > 15. On the number line, what do you draw?
optional.explanation: 'Greater than' (>) is a strict symbol, so 15 is NOT included — open circle. Larger values work, so shade right.
choiceFeedback: Check your operation. Re-read what the problem asks.

optional.stem: (Lesson 7.6) Clue 1: Which value is a solution of x > 7?
optional.explanation: A solution makes x > 7 true. Substitute each: 9 > 7 is true, but 7 > 7, 5 > 7, and 3 > 7 are all false. So 9 is the solution that opens the gate.
choiceFeedback: Check your operation. Re-read what the problem asks.

optional.instructions: (Lesson 7.7) Room 1: The case board is a mess. Sort each clue into whether it needs an EQUATION (one exact total) or an INEQUALITY (a limit or range).

items.text: The ransom was split equally among 5 suspects, giving each $40.
A number of fingerprints plus 9 equals 21.
The getaway car held no more than 6 bags of loot.
The alarm must stay on for at least 30 minutes.
The witness saw fewer than 4 accomplices.
Three identical safes hold exactly 75 coins in all.

optional.hint: Sort by the key operation or concept each item shows.

approaching.stem: (Lesson 7.4) Which inequality represents: 'The temperature is less than 40 degrees'?
approaching.explanation: 'Less than' means <, so the inequality is t < 40.
choiceFeedback: Check your operation. Re-read what the problem asks.
hints: Find the comparison phrase: 'less than 40 degrees'. Does 40 itself count, or only temperatures below it?
'Less than' with no 'or equal to' means a strict symbol — no bar underneath — pointing toward the smaller side.
Test a value: is 35 degrees 'less than 40'? Yes — so pick the strict symbol that puts t on the smaller side of 40.

approaching.stem: (Lesson 7.4) Which inequality represents: 'You must be at least 48 inches tall to ride'?
approaching.explanation: 'At least' means greater than or equal to, so h ≥ 48.
choiceFeedback: Check your operation. Re-read what the problem asks.
hints: 'At least 48' — ask yourself: can a rider who is EXACTLY 48 inches tall ride? That decides whether 48 is included.
When the boundary value is allowed, you need a symbol with the 'or equal to' bar under it.
Allowed heights are 48, 49, 50, and up. Pick the symbol that includes 48 itself AND points toward bigger numbers.

approaching.explanation: x < 5 means 5 is NOT included (open circle) and values less than 5 are shaded (left).
choiceFeedback: Check your operation. Re-read what the problem asks.
hints: Every inequality graph asks two questions: is 5 itself a solution (circle type), and which side holds the solutions (shading)?
Strict symbols like < exclude the boundary, so check whether 5 makes x < 5 true. Then shade toward test values that work.
First step: 5 < 5 is false, so 5 is NOT included — that fixes the circle type. Now test x = 4 to find the shading direction.

approaching.explanation: x ≥ 3 means 3 IS included (closed circle) and values greater than or equal to 3 are shaded (right).
choiceFeedback: Check your operation. Re-read what the problem asks.
hints: Check the symbol: ≥ has the 'or equal' bar. What does that bar mean for the circle at 3?
The bar means 3 IS a solution, so the circle gets filled in. Then a quick test value tells you the shading side.
First step: 3 ≥ 3 is true, so 3 is included. Now test x = 10 — is 10 ≥ 3 true? Shade toward that side.

approaching.explanation: Subtract 6 from both sides: x > 14 − 6 = 8. Graph: open circle at 8, shade right.
choiceFeedback: Check your operation. Re-read what the problem asks.
hints: Solve it like an equation: x has 6 added to it. The > symbol just rides along.
Subtract 6 from both sides — the inequality symbol keeps pointing the same way when you subtract.
Compute 14 − 6 and keep the >. Then test: pick a number bigger than your result and check it makes x + 6 > 14 true.

approaching.explanation: Add 9 to both sides: x ≤ 3 + 9 = 12. Graph: closed circle at 12, shade left.
choiceFeedback: Check your operation. Re-read what the problem asks.
hints: x has 9 subtracted from it. Undo that first; the ≤ symbol keeps its direction.
Add 9 to both sides. Adding the same number to both sides never flips the symbol.
Compute 3 + 9 and keep the ≤. Check by testing a value at or below your boundary in the original inequality.

approaching.stem: (Lesson 7.7) A museum has some paintings. After adding 12, they have 45. Which equation models this?
approaching.explanation: 'Adding 12' to the original number gives 45: p + 12 = 45. Solve: p = 33.
choiceFeedback: Check your operation. Re-read what the problem asks.
hints: The museum STARTS with an unknown number of paintings p, then 12 more are ADDED to reach 45.
'Adding 12' means the model joins p and 12 with a plus sign, and the total 45 goes after the equals sign.
Write the story in order: p, plus 12, equals 45. Which choice matches without switching the operation?

approaching.stem: (Lesson 7.7) A detective needs more than 8 hours to finish the investigation. She has already worked 3 hours. Which inequality represents the additional hours h she needs?
approaching.explanation: 3 hours plus additional hours h must be more than 8: 3 + h > 8. Solve: h > 5.
choiceFeedback: Check your operation. Re-read what the problem asks.
hints: There are two time pieces: the 3 hours already worked and the extra hours h. Together they must pass 8 hours.
'More than 8' means the TOTAL of 3 + h sits on the big side of a strict inequality — not an equals sign.
Combine first: 3 + h. Then compare that total to 8 using the strict 'more than' symbol. Which choice is built that way?

onLevel.label: (Lesson 7.4) Match each situation to its inequality

pairs.situation: A suspect weighs more than 150 pounds.
The detective can spend at most $200 on equipment.
The crime happened fewer than 3 hours ago.
The vault requires at least 5 digit codes.

onLevel.hint: Read each item carefully, then match based on what the problem is asking.
hints: Underline the key phrase in each: 'more than', 'at most', 'fewer than', 'at least'. Two are strict, and two include the boundary number.
Sort first: 'at most' and 'at least' include the number (bar under the symbol); 'more than' and 'fewer than' do not.
Start with the suspect: 'weighs MORE than 150' means strictly above 150 — find the inequality with w and the strict greater-than symbol.

rows.situation: A package weighs less than 50 pounds.
You need at least $25 to buy the game.
No more than 30 students can join the club.

onLevel.label: (Lesson 7.4) Identify the key phrase, symbol, and write the inequality for each situation.
onLevel.hint: Work through each row step by step, checking your answer after each one.
hints: Every row follows the same 3 steps: circle the key phrase, translate it into a symbol, then attach the variable and the number.
Remember: 'less than' is strict, while 'at least' and 'no more than' include the boundary — those two need the 'or equal' bar.
Row 1: the key phrase in 'weighs less than 50 pounds' is 'less than' — put its symbol between w and 50, then treat rows 2 and 3 the same way.

onLevel.label: (Lesson 7.5) Match each inequality to its graph description
onLevel.hint: Read each item carefully, then match based on what the problem is asking.
hints: Split every description into two clues: circle type (open or closed) and shade direction (left or right).
Do circles first: > and < pair with open circles; ≥ and ≤ pair with closed ones. That narrows every match to just two options.
Take x > 10: no 'or equal' bar means an open circle, and solutions are bigger than 10 — find the one description that says both things.

onLevel.instructions: (Lesson 7.5) Read the graph description and write the inequality it represents. Then graph it.

problems.label: Closed circle at 5, shaded right → write the inequality
Open circle at 3, shaded left → write the inequality

hints: Closed circle means ≤ or ≥. Shaded right means greater, so ≥.
Open circle means < or >. Shaded left means less, so <.

onLevel.label: (Lesson 7.6) Solve each inequality, describe the inverse operation, and describe the graph.
onLevel.hint: Work through each row step by step, checking your answer after each one.
hints: Each row is a 3-part job: name the inverse operation, solve for x, then translate the symbol into a circle and shading.
Undo + with − (and − with +) on both sides. Then: ≥ and ≤ mean a closed circle; > and < mean open. Shade the side that makes it true.
Row 1: x + 11 ≥ 20 adds 11, so subtract 11 from both sides and compute 20 − 11. The ≥ means a closed circle; test a big value for the shade side.

onLevel.stem: (Lesson 7.6) Is x = 5 a solution to x + 4 > 12?
choices: No, because 5 + 4 = 9, and 9 is not greater than 12
onLevel.explanation: Substitute: 5 + 4 = 9. Since 9 > 12 is false, x = 5 is NOT a solution.
choiceFeedback: Check your operation. Re-read what the problem asks.
hints: 'Is 5 a solution?' means: substitute 5 for x and see whether the statement comes out TRUE.
Replace x with 5 and compute the left side completely. Then compare that result to 12 honestly — is it really greater?
Compute 5 + 4 first. Then ask: is that total greater than 12? Your yes-or-no needs the correct REASON attached to it.

rows.wordProblem: Five identical boxes weigh a total of 60 pounds. How much does each box weigh?
rows.reasonable: Yes — 12 pounds per box is reasonable.

rows.wordProblem: A shelf can hold at most 30 books. There are already 17 books. How many more can be added?
rows.reasonable: Yes — up to 13 more books fits.

rows.wordProblem: A baker split 84 cookies equally into bags of 12. How many bags did she use?

onLevel.label: (Lesson 7.7) Write a model, solve, and check reasonableness for each problem.
onLevel.hint: Work through each row step by step, checking your answer after each one.
hints: For each row: find the numbers, decide the operation from the story's clue words, then ask if the answer makes real-world sense.
Equal groups (boxes, bags) point to a multiplication model; 'at most' points to an inequality with the 'or equal' bar. Solve with the inverse operation.
Row 1: five EQUAL boxes total 60 pounds — write a multiplication model with w, then divide both sides by 5. Is that weight per box sensible?

onLevel.stem: (Lesson 7.7) A student solved 4n = 52 and got n = 13. Is the answer reasonable if n represents the number of notebooks in a box?
choices: Yes — 13 notebooks per box is reasonable
Yes — but only if n is a fraction
onLevel.explanation: 4 × 13 = 52 ✓. 13 notebooks per box is a reasonable whole number answer.
choiceFeedback: Check your operation. Re-read what the problem asks.
hints: 'Reasonable' asks two things: does the math check out, AND does the number make sense for notebooks in a box?
Check the math first: multiply 4 by 13 and see if it rebuilds 52. Then judge whether that count fits a real box of notebooks.
Compute 4 × 13. Does it equal 52? Then ask: could a box realistically hold that many notebooks? Match your reasoning to one choice.

extending.title: (Lesson 7.4) Find the Inequality Error

workedExample.label: Situation
workedExample.work: No more than 25 students can join the field trip

extending.correctWork: 'No more than' means less than or equal to (≤), not greater than. The correct inequality is s ≤ 25.
hints: 'No more than 25' means the number cannot exceed 25. Is that greater than or less than or equal to?
'No more than' = at most = ≤. The correct inequality is s ≤ 25.

extending.title: (Lesson 7.5) Find the Graphing Error
extending.correctWork: x > 6 uses a strict inequality (no 'equal to'), so the circle should be OPEN, not closed. Open circle at 6, shaded right.
hints: Look at the inequality symbol carefully. Is it > or ≥?
> means strictly greater than — 6 is NOT included, so the circle must be open.

extending.title: (Lesson 7.6) Find the Solving Error
extending.correctWork: The inverse of subtracting 8 is ADDING 8, not subtracting. Add 8 to both sides: x ≥ 15 + 8 = 23. Graph: closed circle at 23, shade right.
hints: The equation has − 8. What is the inverse of subtracting 8?
To undo − 8, you add 8 to both sides: x ≥ 15 + 8 = 23.

extending.title: (Lesson 7.7) Find the Problem-Solving Error

workedExample.label: Problem
workedExample.work: A parking lot holds at most 200 cars. There are 134 already. How many more can park?

extending.correctWork: 'At most' means less than or equal to, so the model should be an inequality: 134 + c ≤ 200. Solving: c ≤ 66. Up to 66 more cars can park, not exactly 66.
hints: The problem says 'at most 200.' Does that mean exactly 200 or up to 200?
'At most' requires ≤, not =. The correct model is 134 + c ≤ 200, so c ≤ 66.

optionalActivity.name: Catch-Up Challenge
optionalActivity.intro: Mix it up: pick the right lesson's big idea for each problem — that's the real catch-up skill.

practice.commonMistake: A common mistake in Equations and Inequalities Problem Solving is matching the wrong model to a key phrase. For 'the getaway car held no more than 6 bags,' students often write the equation b = 6 instead of the inequality b ≤ 6, because they see one number and assume it must be exact. The same mistake happens in reverse: for 'the reward split equally among 5 people gave each $40,' students sometimes write the inequality 5p ≥ 40 instead of the equation 5p = 40, because 'split equally' sounds like it could mean a range. Before you submit, ask: does this phrase give one exact value (equation, =) or a limit/range (inequality, <, >, ≤, ≥)?

diagram.title: Detective's Budget Limit
diagram.caption: She has spent $320 of her $500 cap (closed dot = allowed), so the gap up to $500 shows r ≤ 180 — at most $180 more.

connect.scenario: A detective has a $500 budget for equipment. She has already spent $320. The inequality 320 + r ≤ 500 represents the remaining amount r she can spend. She also needs exactly 4 flashlights at $15 each, represented by the equation 4f = 60.
connect.promptQuestion: How much more can the detective spend? How much does each flashlight cost? When do you use an equation versus an inequality?
connect.prompt: The detective can spend at most $__ more because r ≤ 500 − ___ = ___. Each flashlight costs $__ because f = 60 ÷ ___ = ___.

exitTicket.stem: (Catch-up check, from Lesson 7.5) How would you graph the inequality x ≥ 9?
exitTicket.explanation: x ≥ 9 means 9 is included (closed circle) and values are 9 or greater (shaded right).
choiceFeedback: '≥' includes 9, so the circle should be filled/closed.
x ≥ 9 means 9 and up — shade toward larger numbers.
Both parts are off — '≥' is a closed circle, shaded right.
hints: Break the graph into two decisions: is 9 itself a solution, and which direction do the solutions go?
The 'or equal' bar means the boundary counts — that sets your circle type. Then test a bigger number to find the shading.
First check 9 ≥ 9 — true or false? That decides the circle. Then test x = 12 to see which side of 9 gets shaded.
